$comment: The performance budget, enforced by tools/perf-budget.mjs on every push.
docs/performance-budget.md explains where each number comes from and what
is and is not measured yet. Change a budget there and here together.

referenceMachine.label: mid-range laptop, 2026
referenceMachine.cpu: 4 physical cores, ~2.4 GHz sustained, no discrete GPU
referenceMachine.browser: current Chrome or Firefox, cold HTTP cache, warm DNS
referenceMachine.note: Deliberately not a developer machine. The atlas is for clinicians and students on institutional hardware.

comment: Byte budgets are converted to time with an explicit, stated model rather
than a hand-wave: one RTT to connect, one RTT per round of requests, then
bytes at the downlink rate. HTTP/2 over a static host serves the whole
critical path in one round of requests.
The model is pessimistic about bandwidth (no compression beyond gzip, no
CDN edge) and optimistic about nothing. It is a budget, not a prediction.

bundleGzipBytes.why: 150 KiB is the point at which a 25 Mbit/s link spends more time on our own code than on a round trip. Past that the page shell, not the network, is the thing to fix.

indexGzipBytes.why: The prebuilt indexes are on the critical path for first interaction, so they are capped well below the asset budget. 256 KiB holds the full ALC-1 level and frame tables with room for a label index per frame.

lowResAssetGzipBytes.covers: dist/assets/**, gzipped, excluding LICENSE, ATTRIBUTION.md, the name index and every file a mesh set declares as lazily fetched
lowResAssetGzipBytes.why: 2.5 MiB at 25 Mbit/s is ~0.84 s of transfer, which fits the 2.5 s low-resolution asset budget with room for parse. It is also about the size a 20k-triangle body shell plus label sets lands at, so it constrains the asset pipeline without being unachievable.

lowResBrainAssetGzipBytes.covers: dist/assets/brain/**, gzipped, less the lazily fetched tier: the brain's share of lowResAssetGzipBytes, counted in that line as well
lowResBrainAssetGzipBytes.why: The 2.5 MiB low-resolution line is shared by the brain (DOG-127, W2) and the full-body human (DOG-128, W3). The split, agreed in W2 and recorded in docs/performance-budget.md: brain 1.00 MiB, body 1.25 MiB, and 0.25 MiB for the v1 templates and labels (about 0.13 MiB today). The body gets the larger share because it has more structures to show at once. This line holds the brain to its share, so a brain that grows cannot spend the body's room.

fullResBrainAssetGzipBytes.covers: the brain mesh files declared `loading: "lazy"` in their structures.json (the full-resolution tier), gzipped
fullResBrainAssetGzipBytes.why: Derived once, on 2026-10-11, from the first full-tier build (DOG-127, 4,972,008 B gzip): 1.10 x that, rounded up to the next 256 KiB, = 5.25 MiB. It is a committed literal, not re-derived at gate time, so it cannot ratchet to whatever the next build happens to weigh. At 25 Mbit/s it is about 1.8 s of background transfer after the low tier is already drawn. The 10% was margin for re-encoding the set it was derived from. The origin-test moves (midbrain x2 from the glb, the corpus callosum from BodyParts3D) then added about 349 KB, and holding the 4 colliculi took some of it back, so the 244 structures that ship now leave about 3.6%, not 10% (docs/brain-mesh-report.md has the current reading). The literal stays as derived. Adding a clearance group (the cortex, if it clears) is a new decision about this line, not headroom inside it.

lowResBodyAssetGzipBytes.covers: dist/assets/body/**, gzipped, less the lazily fetched tier: the body's share of lowResAssetGzipBytes, counted in that line as well
lowResBodyAssetGzipBytes.why: The body's 1.25 MiB of the 2.5 MiB low-resolution line, as agreed in W2 (DOG-127) and recorded in docs/performance-budget.md: brain 1.00 MiB, body 1.25 MiB, v1 templates and labels 0.25 MiB. It holds the full-body human (DOG-128, W3) to its share, so a body that grows cannot spend the brain's room.

fullResBodyAssetGzipBytes.covers: the body mesh files declared `loading: "lazy"` in their structures.json (the full-resolution tier), gzipped
fullResBodyAssetGzipBytes.why: Derived once, on 2026-10-12, from the first body full tier that passed the mesh gate (DOG-128 at 34196ea, 6,525,597 B gzip), by the brain's rule: 1.10 x that, rounded up to the next 256 KiB, = 7.00 MiB. A committed literal, not re-derived at gate time, so it cannot ratchet. At 25 Mbit/s it is about 2.3 s of background transfer after the low tier has drawn. The full tier is itself decimated (source 6.4 million triangles is ~46 MB), except the 25 BD vertebrae, which ship at source resolution because the registration gate measures BD from them.

indexParseMsNormalised.covers: JSON.parse of data/*.json plus building the lookup maps, normalised to the reference machine
indexParseMsNormalised.why: Main-thread work before the page can respond. 40 ms keeps it inside one frame budget's worth of slack on a 60 Hz display even after layout.

nameIndexBuildMsNormalised.covers: step 1 of app.js: assets/labels/names.json joined with coverings.json through joinNameIndex() and buildNameIndex(), which calls covering() once per structure, over the documents the build emitted. Found through the atlas index's own nameIndex descriptor, the way app.js finds it. Normalised to the reference machine.
nameIndexBuildMsNormalised.why: Boot-time main-thread work the page awaits before it can answer a click, so what it has to fit inside is FIRST INTERACTION and not one 60 Hz frame — nothing is painted yet, so no frame is being dropped. The ceiling is 5% of derivedFirstInteractionMs (5% of 3500 ms = 175 ms): the index may have a twentieth of the first-visit budget and no more, because the rest is transfer, parse and the viewer's first paint. Derived by DOG-98's rule, roundUpTo10(1.5 x this gate's own best-of-N reading), capped at that 175 ms. The reading is 64.2 ms, the highest of 22 runs of this gate on the branch this landed on: roundUpTo10(1.5 x 64.2 = 96.2) = 100, under the cap, so the cap does not bind. docs/performance-budget.md records the whole sample and the arithmetic. The 1.5x is for spread rather than slack — those 22 runs read between 26 ms and 64 ms, and almost all of that is the calibration's own noise, not the index's — because a limit set at the reading flaps red on a contended runner, which is how a line ends up switched off. The worst combination actually observed, the slowest build against the fastest calibration, is 77.8 ms: 78% of this limit. The figure gated here is a best-of-15, which is the machine's capability and not what a user pays; the cold first attempt runs about twice as long and is reported beside it, so this line and derivedFirstInteractionMs are both optimistic about this term by about that factor.

nameIndexBuildUsPerCell.covers: the same measurement as nameIndexBuildMsNormalised, divided by the number of cells the index binds (the sum of coverings[].cells, reported as nameIndex.cells)
nameIndexBuildUsPerCell.why: The invariant the absolute line cannot carry. Today's 57 structures and 3478 cells are the smallest index v1 will ever bind, so an absolute limit is consumed by growth and says less every time the atlas gets bigger, while a per-cell limit cannot be. It is also what stops DOG-80's quadratic covering() coming back: a quadratic prune reds this line at any scale, where the absolute line would only notice once the index was big enough. Derived by DOG-98's rule, roundUpTo2(1.5 x reading / cells), from the same 64.2 ms reading as the line above: roundUpTo2(1.5 x 64.2 / 3478 = 27.7 us) = 28. At today's 3478 cells that is 97.4 ms, marginally TIGHTER than the 100 ms absolute line, because the two roundings land differently — so at this scale a per-cell regression is what reds first, and the absolute line only leads once the index has grown. Over here means the cost of binding one cell moved, which is a real regression in covering() or the join; over on the absolute line alone means the index grew, and the gate says so itself.

lowResAssetParseMsNormalised.covers: Parsing the low-resolution asset payloads and walking their positions and indices once, normalised to the reference machine: JSON.parse for JSON assets, the ATLM reader (tools/lib/meshbin.mjs) for binary meshes
lowResAssetParseMsNormalised.why: Off the critical path for first interaction but on it for seeing anything. The viewer is expected to move this to a worker; until it does, 400 ms is the ceiling.

derivedLowResAssetLoadMs.covers: navigation start to low-resolution geometry parsed and ready, on the reference machine, derived from the byte and parse budgets through the transfer model
derivedLowResAssetLoadMs.why: The number a user feels. Under 2.5 s an atlas feels like a document; over it, like an application that is loading.

derivedFirstInteractionMs.covers: navigation start to the first click being handled, on the reference machine, derived as above plus a fixed render allowance
derivedFirstInteractionMs.why: Interaction is the product. 3.5 s is the outer edge of acceptable for a first visit to a 3D atlas, and the target to beat once the viewer lands.

derivedFirstBrainFrameMs.covers: a brain link, navigation start to the first brain frame drawn, on the reference machine: the critical path of derivedFirstInteractionMs, one round of asset requests, the files the page fetches for the brain (each brain mesh set's structures.json, label file and registration where declared, and its eager tier, read from the atlas index's meshSets), the viewer's own decode of them (meshSetFrom, normalised), and the render allowance
derivedFirstBrainFrameMs.why: DOG-123 set the first brain frame at <= 3,500 ms modelled on this reference machine, as the derivedFirstInteractionMs limit, with no loosened line (CTO comment of 2026-10-11 17:02, carried into DOG-129). That line's derivation stops at the critical path, so it cannot see the brain at all; this one prices the brain in, under the same 3,500 ms. It is a second line at the same limit, not a looser one.

comment: A line at 98% of its limit is green, and is one small addition away from
red. The gate used to say nothing about the difference: every budget was
either met or busted, and the room left over was not reported at all.
Any line at or above this fraction of its limit is now reported as TIGHT on
a run that still passes. This is NOT a second limit. It changes no verdict
and no exit status, and it cannot fail a build. It exists so that the cost
of filling a budget falls on the change that fills it, instead of on the
next person to touch the page — who would otherwise meet the line as a red
build for a change that was not the one that spent the room.
Raising this fraction to quiet a warning accomplishes nothing: it hides the
notice and leaves the limit, and the shortage, exactly where they were. The
thing that must not happen is raising a LIMIT to make a change fit. See
docs/performance-budget.md, 'Changing a budget'.
0.9 leaves one tenth of the line. On bundleGzipBytes that is 15 KiB, which
is larger than any single module the page shell has gained so far, so a
line crossing this threshold still has about one addition of room — enough
warning to be able to act on it, which is the whole point of warning.

renderAllowanceMs.comment: Fixed allowance for layout, first paint and the viewer's first GPU upload on the reference machine. A placeholder with a stated basis, not a measurement: it needs the viewer and a real browser to measure. Flagged as such in every report.

comment: CI runners are not mid-range laptops and their speed varies run to run,
so a raw parse time measured in CI cannot be compared to a budget stated
for a laptop. This fixed workload is run alongside the measurement and
used to normalise it:
normalised = measured * (referenceMs / observedCalibrationMs)
referenceMs is what the workload takes on the reference machine. It is a
single scalar and a crude one: it corrects for clock speed and little
else. Raw and normalised numbers are both always reported.
min/maxSpeedFactor bound where the correction is small enough to quote a
normalised number: past them the normalisation would be doing more work
than the measurement. Outside the band the gate does NOT quote one and
does NOT fail. It reports the unnormalised time as a one-sided bound —
a lower bound on a runner faster than the reference, an upper bound on a
slower one — and gates only in the direction that bound settles. Byte
budgets never touch the calibration and stay exact and hard either way.
Widening the band is not the way to make a fast runner green; it quotes
a bigger correction as if it were a measurement. The evidence that would
justify it is a measured distribution of this workload across the runner
pool, not a single reading. See docs/performance-budget.md.
